entities.name: Iglesia de los Santos Justo y Pastor, Toledo
entities.label: Institution
entities.summary:
The Church of Saints Justus and Pastor (Iglesia de los Santos Justo y Pastor) in Toledo, Spain, is a historic Catholic church dedicated to Saints Justus and Pastor, two child martyrs from Alcalá de Henares who were executed during the Diocletian persecution (circa 304 CE) and are the patron saints of Alcalá and of the Complutense University tradition — with their cult spreading throughout Castile and their dedication in Toledo churches reflecting the early Christian martyrdom tradition that deeply shaped Iberian Catholic identity.

Saints Justus and Pastor (San Justo y Pastor) were legendary child martyrs of approximately 13 and 7 years old who, according to hagiographic tradition, voluntarily presented themselves to the Roman governor in Alcalá de Henares (then Complutum) to be martyred after hearing of others being executed for Christianity. Their youth, courage, and voluntary martyrdom made them powerful symbols of Christian commitment; their cult was well established by the 4th century and their feast day (August 6) was observed throughout the Iberian Church.

The Toledo church dedicated to Saints Justus and Pastor reflects the dense network of martyr-saint dedications in Toledo's ecclesiastical geography. Toledo's churches collectively preserve the memory of the entire range of early Christian martyrdom traditions, both local (Santa Leocadia) and regional (Saints Justus and Pastor from nearby Alcalá). Toledo's extraordinary religious concentration — with hundreds of historic churches in a small walled city — makes each dedication part of a continuous liturgical memory of Iberian Christianity extending from the Roman period through the Reconquista to the present.

historicalSignificance.significanceNarrative: The Church of Saints Justus and Pastor Toledo — dedicated to Castile's beloved child martyrs, part of Toledo's extraordinary ecclesiastical network, and preserving memory of the Diocletian persecution's Iberian victims — is historically meaningful as a node in early Iberian Christian martyrdom commemoration.
